summary:
Walking into Space, developed by Team Gumj, is an interactive educational simulation platform designed to overcome the difficulty of experiencing actual extraterrestrial environments and the general lack of understanding regarding space facilities. Aspiring future astronauts often struggle to grasp how planetary bases survive unpredictable cosmic hazards. To solve this challenge, our project immerses users in realistic virtual environments featuring Mars and Venus, where they must actively respond to severe planetary disasters such as extreme temperature fluctuations, Martian dust storms, ultra-high atmospheric pressure, and corrosive sulfuric acid clouds. 
Through an intuitive card-selection gameplay mechanism, players explore and operate scientifically grounded disaster-response facilities—including Electrodynamic Dust Shields, Mechanically Pumped Fluid Loops, Fluorinated Ethylene Propylene coatings, and High-Pressure Resistant Systems. Players make strategic engineering choices and immediately observe how their decisions impact base integrity and solar energy production. This project is vitally important because it bridges the gap between theoretical space science and practical crisis management, inspiring and educating the next generation of space explorers by transforming complex aerospace engineering principles into an engaging, hands-on virtual experience.
details:
We are students at a National Meister School, where we learn by building and handling real work rather than stopping at theory. While looking at the technologies we study in class, we became interested in the fact that NASA’s exploration equipment is also a single system in which power, communications, thermal control and sensors work together. As we researched how probes and rovers survive in extreme environments, we wanted to rebuild these principles with the skills we have learned and let anyone experience them. Space science often feels difficult and distant, and we judged that a game where players choose, see the consequences and learn, instead of memorizing, could close that gap. That is why we started this project.

“Walking into Space” is a space-survival simulation that teaches real NASA exploration instruments and science. Players act as student crew members facing crises at Venus and Mars bases, chapter by chapter, and solve them by choosing equipment cards. Players manage power, solar output, oxygen, life support, thermal control, communications, water, data, trust and science score. Choices cascade across systems: low power, for example, also weakens communications and life support. The highest number is therefore not always the right answer, and players must weigh earlier choices together with the current situation. Picking science-analysis cards unlocks hidden cards, and play ends in one of seven endings. Every card is labeled as a real mission, research stage or fictional so players can tell fact from imagination, and the explanations draw on NASA material such as Magellan radar, SuperCam, Mastcam-Z and the EDS dust-removal technology.

The benefit is that learners understand space science by choosing and seeing consequences rather than memorizing. Each result screen explains the scientific principle behind the outcome, and the game runs in a browser with no installation or sign-up. For us, it became a hands-on experience of solving problems from start to finish. Our goal is to add new planets to the data structure, expanding the story to the Moon or Jupiter’s moons, and to develop it into learning content that other students can use to experience space science.

For design, we chose a dark space theme with only the key information on each screen, and danger is signaled intuitively by an alarm glow at the screen edges. The layout is responsive so it works comfortably on phones. The project is built with HTML, CSS, JavaScript and React 18. Background music is synthesized with the Web Audio API, and progress is saved in the browser’s localStorage. Any PC or smartphone with a web browser can run it. The code, scenario text, score data and audio-synthesis code were written with the help of the generative AI Claude (Anthropic), while the Mars base image and EDS diagram are AI-generated and watermarked.
